statements.text: Here is the problem. It is someone else or some artificial intelligence algorithm that has inordinate power to subjectively combine strategic data with strategic audiences to shape whatever thoughts and news they want.
statements.context: House Energy and Commerce Committee hearing on TikTok's data privacy and child safety practices, with CEO Shou Zi Chew testifying.

statements.text: Mr. Schulman, one of the topics we have talked about a lot in this committee has to do with artificial intelligence, and just listening to the joint comments of the panel today, we have talked about the helpful side of artificial intelligence. [...] There are some really positive employments for artificial intelligence, but frankly, there are some components to that that scare me. The potential algorithms that are focused on shaping, that type of thing. But it all has to draw from a database, and so I am wondering with blockchain employing a decentralized data storage, is there a role for blockchain when it comes to potentially neutralizing some of the—what could be the negative impacts of artificial intelligence?
statements.context: House subcommittee hearing on blockchain and distributed ledger technologies, where a member shifts the discussion to AI risks and potential technical mitigations.

statements.text: We need to know how AI can help predict machine failures better to prevent production interruptions. [...] We need to understand how to provide for data sharing for these needs while ensuring privacy among our end users.
statements.context: Opening statement at a House subcommittee hearing on AI in manufacturing and U.S. competitiveness.

statements.text: In your testimony you said there's three things Congress should do in order to move forward regarding AI. The second point you made was one Federal AI standard. [...] Specifically, what should those standards be, to the best of your advice?
statements.context: House committee hearing on AI technology and American competitiveness, where Representative Fulcher questions a witness about proposed federal AI standards.

statements.text: Then peeling the onion back, we believe that we need to create a regulatory framework that enables innovation while still adding some level of guardrails.
statements.context: Congressional hearing on AI technology and American competitiveness where a private-sector witness (Mr. Wang) responds to a question from Rep. Fulcher.

statements.text: I would like to talk about the different approaches to AI regulation and ensuring that U.S. companies don't face unfair barriers to selling their products and services abroad.
statements.context: House hearing on AI Regulation and the Future of U.S. Leadership, questioning a witness panel.

statements.text: In the face of Chinese progress in emerging technologies, I am concerned about the U.S.'s ability to maintain its leadership position—if, in fact, we still have one, and I would like to get your opinion on that—in the AI race, especially if we were to follow the European approach, which I don't see us doing, or allow a patchwork of AI rules to develop across the various States.
statements.context: House hearing on AI regulation and U.S. leadership where Representative Fulcher questions a witness about strategic competition with China in AI.

statements.text: What we don't want happening is a chatbot taking the role of teaching a child right and wrong. [...] are you concerned that children may look up upon or to a faceless chatbot as a sort of parental authority or ﬁgure, and how do we propose that parents and educators prevent that from happening?
statements.context: House hearing titled 'Innovation with Integrity: Examining the Risks and Benefits of AI Chatbots'; Rep. Fulcher questioning a witness.
